title: Fully alive
hook: Irenaeus: the glory of God is a human being fully alive

segments.voice: Yesterday, Perpetua and Felicity, and your line was sisters. Whose hand did you offer, literally or not? Day seven hundred sixty.

A few days ago we met Polycarp, the old bishop who wouldn't curse Christ. Here's a thread from that story. A man named Irenaeus writes that he saw Polycarp in his own early youth. He remembers him. Irenaeus grows up to be a bishop himself, and to write a long, careful book against teachings he believes are pulling Christians away from the faith they received. It's a big, argumentative book, full of names and systems. And somewhere in the middle of it sits one short line that people still quote today. The line is today's word.

The line, in its old Latin text, reads gloria Dei vivens homo. Word for word: the glory of God, a living human being. Some modern versions render it the glory of God is a human being fully alive. The words fully alive are a translator's way of bringing out the force of vivens, living. They aren't separate words in the Latin. And the sentence keeps going. Irenaeus adds, in paraphrase: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. So it's a circle. God is glorified when people are truly alive, and people are truly alive when they see God. Why would anyone need to say that? Because some teachers in Irenaeus's world taught that the physical world was a mistake, that the body was a prison, and that real spiritual life meant escaping it. Irenaeus pushes back hard. The one God made the world, he says, and made it good. God works with dust and breath, and the Son of God took on flesh. It's the note the Bible strikes in its first chapter: "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." For Irenaeus, being human isn't a problem to be solved. It's what God is bringing to life. Christians hear the line in different ways. Some hear it as joy: God delights in people who are awake, creative, glad to be in a body. Others are quick to add the second half, so that fully alive never just means busy or thrilled. For Irenaeus, the deepest life is seeing God. Both halves belong to the one sentence. Neither is the whole without the other.
screen: `AND THE LIFE OF HUMANS: SEEING GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing that makes you fully alive. Settle, and breathe. Notice that you're in a body: feet, hands, the weight of you in the chair. Now let your mind go to something that wakes you up. Not something that keeps you busy. Something that makes you more yourself. Cooking for people. Walking under trees. Singing badly. Fixing a thing. Pick one you could do today, even for ten minutes. If you pray, you can offer it to God as a thank you. If you don't, just hold it, and look forward to it. The bell holds the time.
Fully alive. From Irenaeus: the glory of God is a living human being, and the life of a human being is the vision of God.
Your line: fully alive. Today, do the one thing you picked, on purpose, and notice what it wakes up in you. Day seven hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Some Christians quote Irenaeus's line in sermons, retreats and books about prayer and creativity, and some pair it with its second half, that the life of a human being is the vision of God.

notes: Against Heresies 4.20.7 Latin: 'Gloria enim Dei vivens homo, vita autem hominis visio Dei.' The script says 'its old Latin text' without making claims about the lost Greek original; confirm wording and pronunciation.
'Fully alive' is presented as a modern rendering of 'vivens'; the Roberts-Donaldson (ANF) translation reads roughly 'the glory of God is a living man'. Paraphrased, not quoted.
Irenaeus saw Polycarp 'in my early youth' (AH 3.3.4); the hook says 'in his own early youth'. Confirm the backward link to day 756 (Polycarp) is accurate.
The teachers Irenaeus opposed (usually called Gnostics) are described in general terms ('the physical world was a mistake, the body a prison'); confirm this is fair and not a caricature.
The script does not say where Irenaeus was bishop; Lyon is the usual answer but comes from other sources.
